claim: Budding yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) accumulates protein aggregates containing oxidatively damaged proteins during aging.
source: Disrupted protein homeostasis results in the accumulation of protein aggregates that contain oxidatively damaged proteins (Aguilaniu et al., 2003; Erjavec et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Aguilaniu et al., 2003; Erjavec et al., 2007).

claim: During aging in budding yeast, mitochondria fragment and aggregate.
source: Many organelles exhibit signs of dysfunction: mitochondria fragment and aggregate, mitochondrial membrane potential decreases, and the vacuole becomes less acidic (Henderson et al., 2014; Hughes and Gottschling, 2012; Veatch et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Henderson et al., 2014; Hughes and Gottschling, 2012; Veatch et al., 2009).

claim: During aging in budding yeast, mitochondrial membrane potential decreases.
source: Many organelles exhibit signs of dysfunction: mitochondria fragment and aggregate, mitochondrial membrane potential decreases, and the vacuole becomes less acidic (Henderson et al., 2014; Hughes and Gottschling, 2012; Veatch et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Henderson et al., 2014; Hughes and Gottschling, 2012; Veatch et al., 2009).

claim: During aging in budding yeast, the vacuole becomes less acidic.
source: Many organelles exhibit signs of dysfunction: mitochondria fragment and aggregate, mitochondrial membrane potential decreases, and the vacuole becomes less acidic (Henderson et al., 2014; Hughes and Gottschling, 2012; Veatch et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Henderson et al., 2014; Hughes and Gottschling, 2012; Veatch et al., 2009).

claim: The nucleolus enlarges during aging in budding yeast.
source: Notably, the nucleus also undergoes a number of changes including enlargement of the nucleolus (Lewinska et al., 2014; Morlot et al., 2019; Sinclair et al., 1997), misorganization of nuclear pore complexes (Lord et al., 2015; Rempel et al., 2019), and accumulation of extrachromosomal ribosomal DNA (rDNA) circles (Denoth-Lippuner et al., 2014; Sinclair and Guarente, 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Lewinska et al., 2014; Morlot et al., 2019; Sinclair et al., 1997).

claim: Nuclear pore complexes become misorganized during aging in budding yeast.
source: Notably, the nucleus also undergoes a number of changes including enlargement of the nucleolus (Lewinska et al., 2014; Morlot et al., 2019; Sinclair et al., 1997), misorganization of nuclear pore complexes (Lord et al., 2015; Rempel et al., 2019), and accumulation of extrachromosomal ribosomal DNA (rDNA) circles (Denoth-Lippuner et al., 2014; Sinclair and Guarente, 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Lord et al., 2015; Rempel et al., 2019).

claim: Extrachromosomal ribosomal DNA (rDNA) circles accumulate during aging in budding yeast.
source: Notably, the nucleus also undergoes a number of changes including enlargement of the nucleolus (Lewinska et al., 2014; Morlot et al., 2019; Sinclair et al., 1997), misorganization of nuclear pore complexes (Lord et al., 2015; Rempel et al., 2019), and accumulation of extrachromosomal ribosomal DNA (rDNA) circles (Denoth-Lippuner et al., 2014; Sinclair and Guarente, 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Denoth-Lippuner et al., 2014; Sinclair and Guarente, 1997).

claim: Many cellular changes that occur with age in budding yeast are conserved across eukaryotes.
source: Many of the cellular changes that accrue with age are conserved across eukaryotes (Colacurcio and Nixon, 2016; David et al., 2010; Sun et al., 2016; Tiku et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Colacurcio and Nixon, 2016; David et al., 2010; Sun et al., 2016; Tiku et al., 2017).

claim: In budding yeast mitosis, age-induced damage is asymmetrically retained by the mother cell, resulting in an aged mother cell and a young daughter cell.
source: In budding yeast mitosis, age-induced damage is asymmetrically retained by the mother cell resulting in the formation of an aged mother cell and a young daughter cell (Mortimer and Johnston, 1959).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Mortimer and Johnston, 1959).

claim: Meiotic cells in budding yeast reset aging symmetrically such that all meiotic products are born young, independent of their progenitor's age.
source: In contrast, meiotic cells reset aging symmetrically such that all of the meiotic products are born young, independent of their progenitor's age (Unal et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Unal et al., 2011).

claim: Senescence factors including protein aggregates, nucleolar damage, and rDNA circles are no longer present in newly formed gametes in budding yeast.
source: Importantly, senescence factors originally present in the aged precursor cells, including protein aggregates, nucleolar damage, and rDNA circles, are no longer present in the newly formed gametes (Ünal and Amon, 2011; Unal et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Ünal and Amon, 2011; Unal et al., 2011).

claim: The nuclear envelope remains continuous during budding yeast meiosis until karyokinesis forms four new nuclei.
source: In yeast gametogenesis, the nucleus undergoes a closed division, with the nuclear envelope remaining continuous until karyokinesis forms four new nuclei (Moens, 1971; Moens and Rapport, 1971; Neiman, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Moens, 1971; Moens and Rapport, 1971; Neiman, 2011).

claim: New plasma membranes (prospore membranes) grow from the spindle pole bodies during budding yeast meiosis.
source: Around the same time, new plasma membranes, also known as prospore membranes, grow from the centrosome-like spindle pole bodies embedded in the nuclear envelope.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text as a known fact about yeast meiosis.

claim: Directed growth of plasma membrane ensures that nascent nuclei and a fraction of cytoplasmic contents are encapsulated to form gametes in budding yeast.
source: This directed growth of plasma membrane ensures that nascent nuclei and a fraction of the cytoplasmic contents are encapsulated to form gametes (Brewer et al., 1980; Byers, 1981; Knop and Strasser, 2000; Moens, 1971; Neiman, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Brewer et al., 1980; Byers, 1981; Knop and Strasser, 2000; Moens, 1971; Neiman, 1998).

claim: Uninherited cellular contents are destroyed by proteases released upon permeabilization of the progenitor cell's vacuole during budding yeast gametogenesis.
source: Subsequently, the uninherited cellular contents are destroyed by proteases released upon permeabilization of the progenitor cell's vacuole, the yeast equivalent of the mammalian lysosome (Eastwood et al., 2012; Eastwood and Meneghini, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Eastwood et al., 2012; Eastwood and Meneghini, 2015).

claim: Protein aggregates localize to a perinuclear region inside the nucleus prior to meiotic divisions and in meiosis I in aged budding yeast cells.
source: Similar to mitosis, we observed that protein aggregates, visualized by the fluorescently tagged chaperone Hsp104-eGFP (Glover and Lindquist, 1998; Saarikangas et al., 2017), localized to a perinuclear region inside the nucleus prior to the meiotic divisions and in meiosis I (Figure 1B, right panel; Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and by citations to published research (Glover and Lindquist, 1998; Saarikangas et al., 2017).

claim: Protein aggregates are sequestered away from chromosomes during meiosis II in aged budding yeast cells.
source: In contrast, during meiosis II, the protein aggregates localized away from chromosomes, a phenomenon we termed sequestration (Figure 1B and D; Figure 1—source data 1; Video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B, Figure 1D, and Video 1.

claim: Protein aggregate sequestration during meiosis II is highly penetrant (>99%) in aged budding yeast cells.
source: The sequestration was highly penetrant (>99%) and occurred with consistent timing shortly after the onset of anaphase II (Figure 1D; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Protein aggregate sequestration occurs shortly after the onset of anaphase II in aged budding yeast cells.
source: The sequestration was highly penetrant (>99%) and occurred with consistent timing shortly after the onset of anaphase II (Figure 1D; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Sequestered protein aggregates disappear late in gametogenesis in aged budding yeast cells.
source: Subsequently, the aggregates disappeared late in gametogenesis (Figure 1B, right panel; Video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Video 1.

claim: Young budding yeast cells do not contain Hsp104-associated protein aggregates but display diffuse Hsp104 signal throughout meiosis.
source: By comparison, young cells did not contain any Hsp104-associated aggregates but instead displayed diffuse Hsp104 signal throughout meiosis (Figure 1B, left panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Extrachromosomal rDNA circles are sequestered away from dividing chromosomes after the onset of anaphase II in aged budding yeast cells.
source: Using this method, we observed that, in aged cells, a substantial fraction of the tetO-rDNA/TetR-GFP signal and a small fraction of the Hta1-mApple signal were sequestered away from the dividing chromosomes after the onset of anaphase II and disappeared during late stages of gamete maturation (Figure 1C, right panel; Figure 1E; Figure 1—source data 2; Video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C, Figure 1E, and Video 2.

claim: Sequestered extrachromosomal rDNA circles disappear during late stages of gamete maturation in aged budding yeast cells.
source: Using this method, we observed that, in aged cells, a substantial fraction of the tetO-rDNA/TetR-GFP signal and a small fraction of the Hta1-mApple signal were sequestered away from the dividing chromosomes after the onset of anaphase II and disappeared during late stages of gamete maturation (Figure 1C, right panel; Figure 1E; Figure 1—source data 2; Video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C, Figure 1E, and Video 2.

claim: In young budding yeast cells, gamete nuclei retain the entire tetO-rDNA array and histone-bound chromatin after completion of anaphase II.
source: By comparison, in young cells, the gamete nuclei retained the entire tetO-rDNA array and histone-bound chromatin after completion of anaphase II (Figure 1C, left panel), consistent with previous work (Fuchs and Loidl, 2004; Li et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and by citations to published research (Fuchs and Loidl, 2004; Li et al., 2011).

claim: The rRNA processing factor Nsr1 is partially sequestered away from chromosomes during gametogenesis in young budding yeast cells.
source: Nsr1 similarly demonstrated partial sequestration after the onset of anaphase II in young cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Nsr1 foci appear enlarged and fragmented prior to meiotic divisions in aged budding yeast cells.
source: In aged cells, Nsr1 foci appeared enlarged and fragmented prior to the meiotic divisions, consistent with previously reported changes in nucleolar morphology (Figure 2B; Janssens et al., 2015; Morlot et al., 2019; Sinclair et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and by citations to published research (Janssens et al., 2015; Morlot et al., 2019; Sinclair et al., 1997).

claim: Nsr1 is sequestered away from chromosomes following the onset of anaphase II and subsequently eliminated in aged budding yeast cells.
source: As in young cells, Nsr1 was sequestered away from chromosomes following the onset of anaphase II and subsequently eliminated (Figure 2B–C; Figure 2—source data 1; Video 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B, Figure 2C, and Video 3.

claim: A significantly higher fraction of total Nsr1 is sequestered in older budding yeast cells compared to younger cells.
source: Interestingly, a significantly higher fraction of the total Nsr1 was sequestered in older cells (mean = 23% for 0–3 generation-old cells, 36% for 5–8 generation-old cells and 42% for nine or more generation-old cells; Figure 2D; Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: A portion of histone H2B (Htb1-mCherry) is sequestered away from gamete nuclei, predominantly in aged budding yeast cells.
source: A portion of the histone H2B (Htb1-mCherry) was also sequestered away from the gamete nuclei, reminiscent of the behavior of histone H2A in the GFP-marked rDNA strain. This chromatin demarcation occurred predominantly in aged cells and always co-localized with the sequestered nucleoli.
evidence: The claim is based on observations described in the text.

claim: Sequestered extrachromosomal histone signal co-localizes with sequestered nucleoli in aged budding yeast cells.
source: A portion of the histone H2B (Htb1-mCherry) was also sequestered away from the gamete nuclei, reminiscent of the behavior of histone H2A in the GFP-marked rDNA strain. This chromatin demarcation occurred predominantly in aged cells and always co-localized with the sequestered nucleoli.
evidence: The claim is based on observations described in the text.

claim: The timing and location of protein aggregate sequestration coincide with nucleolar sequestration in aged budding yeast cells.
source: Finally, we analyzed the behavior of protein aggregates with respect to nucleoli and found that both the timing and location of the sequestration event were coincident (Figure 2E–F; Figure 2—source data 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2F.

claim: The nucleoporin Nsp1 localizes away from chromosomes in meiosis II in budding yeast.
source: Intriguingly, one nucleoporin, Nsp1, has been previously shown to localize away from chromosomes in meiosis II (Fuchs and Loidl, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Fuchs and Loidl, 2004).

claim: Nucleoporins from five of six tested subcomplexes exhibit sequestration and elimination similar to age-induced damage during budding yeast meiosis.
source: We found that nucleoporins from five of the six tested subcomplexes, including those most integral to the NPC structure, exhibited sequestration and elimination similar to age-induced damage.
evidence: The claim is based on the survey of 17 different nucleoporins described in the text and shown in Figure 3.

claim: Nucleoporins localize to the nuclear periphery before meiotic divisions and during meiosis I, but largely localize away from chromosomes after the onset of anaphase II in budding yeast.
source: The nucleoporins localized to the nuclear periphery before the meiotic divisions and during meiosis I, but largely localized away from chromosomes after the onset of anaphase II (Figure 3B–F; Figure 3—figure supplements 1–5; Video 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B–F, Figure 3—figure supplements 1–5, and Video 4.

claim: Some nucleoporins re-appear around gamete nuclei during budding yeast meiosis, either by de novo synthesis or return of the pre-existing pool.
source: Although a large fraction of the nucleoporins persisted away from the chromosomes, some nucleoporins re-appeared around the gamete nuclei, either by de novo synthesis or return of the pre-existing pool.
evidence: The claim is based on observations described in the text and shown in Figure 3.

claim: Remaining nucleoporin signal outside of gamete nuclei abruptly disappears several hours after meiotic divisions in budding yeast.
source: Several hours after the meiotic divisions, any remaining nucleoporin signal outside of the gamete nuclei abruptly disappeared (Figure 3B–F; Figure 3—figure supplements 1–5; Video 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B–F, Figure 3—figure supplements 1–5, and Video 4.

claim: Nuclear basket nucleoporins briefly localize outside of developing nuclei during anaphase II but largely return to nascent nuclei within 30 minutes in budding yeast.
source: Interestingly, the nucleoporins from one subcomplex, the nuclear basket, exhibited a markedly different behavior: although briefly localizing outside of the developing nuclei during anaphase II along with the nucleoporins from other subcomplexes, they largely returned to the nascent nuclei within 30 min (Figure 3G–H; Figure 3—figure supplement 6; Video 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G–H, Figure 3—figure supplement 6, and Video 5.

claim: The nuclear basket detaches from the rest of the NPC during meiosis II in budding yeast.
source: The simplest interpretation of these findings was that the nuclear basket detached from the rest of the NPC during meiosis II.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on the observed behavior of nuclear basket nucleoporins.

claim: Intact NPCs without nuclear baskets are left outside of gamete nuclei during budding yeast meiosis.
source: Given that all other NPC subcomplexes tested persist outside of developing nuclei, we propose that intact NPCs without nuclear baskets are left outside of gamete nuclei.
evidence: The claim is a proposal based on the observed behavior of different NPC subcomplexes.

claim: Protein aggregates, rDNA circles, and sequestered nucleolar material co-localize with sequestered NPCs after the onset of anaphase II in budding yeast.
source: We monitored the localization of protein aggregates, rDNA circles, and sequestered nucleolar material relative to NPCs and found that they co-localize with the sequestered NPCs after the onset of anaphase II (Figure 4A–C; Figure 4—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A–C and Figure 4—figure supplements 1–2.

claim: The integral LEM-domain protein Heh1 localizes to both nascent gamete nuclei and sequestered NPCs during anaphase II in budding yeast.
source: We found that the integral LEM-domain protein Heh1 (Gene ID: 854974) and a generic inner nuclear membrane (INM) marker, eGFP-h2NLS-L-TM, localized to both nascent gamete nuclei and the sequestered NPCs during anaphase II (Figure 5A–B; Figure 5—figure supplement 1; King et al., 2006; Meinema et al., 2011), suggesting the existence of a separate membranous compartment.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A–B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1, and by citations to published research (King et al., 2006; Meinema et al., 2011).

claim: A generic inner nuclear membrane marker (eGFP-h2NLS-L-TM) localizes to both nascent gamete nuclei and sequestered NPCs during anaphase II in budding yeast.
source: We found that the integral LEM-domain protein Heh1 (Gene ID: 854974) and a generic inner nuclear membrane (INM) marker, eGFP-h2NLS-L-TM, localized to both nascent gamete nuclei and the sequestered NPCs during anaphase II (Figure 5A–B; Figure 5—figure supplement 1; King et al., 2006; Meinema et al., 2011), suggesting the existence of a separate membranous compartment.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A–B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1, and by citations to published research (King et al., 2006; Meinema et al., 2011).

claim: A separate membranous compartment exists outside of gamete nuclei during budding yeast meiosis II.
source: We found that the integral LEM-domain protein Heh1 (Gene ID: 854974) and a generic inner nuclear membrane (INM) marker, eGFP-h2NLS-L-TM, localized to both nascent gamete nuclei and the sequestered NPCs during anaphase II (Figure 5A–B; Figure 5—figure supplement 1; King et al., 2006; Meinema et al., 2011), suggesting the existence of a separate membranous compartment.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the localization of inner nuclear membrane proteins to both gamete nuclei and sequestered NPCs.

claim: Serial section transmission electron microscopy confirms the existence of nuclear envelope-bound space outside of the four nuclei during budding yeast meiosis.
source: Reconstructions of individual cells, either during anaphase II or during gamete development, confirmed the existence of nuclear envelope-bound space outside of the four nuclei (Figure 5C–D; Videos 6–9).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5C–D and Videos 6–9.

claim: The nuclear envelope-bound compartment outside of gamete nuclei appears deformed with abnormal membrane structure and is often fragmented in budding yeast meiosis.
source: The compartment seemed deformed in comparison to the nascent gamete nuclei in that the nuclear envelope membrane structure appeared abnormal and the compartment was often fragmented into multiple nuclear envelope-bound regions (Figure 5C–5F; Videos 6–9).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5C–5F and Videos 6–9.

claim: The nuclear envelope-bound compartment outside of gamete nuclei is located outside of the gamete plasma membranes in budding yeast meiosis.
source: These regions were located outside of the gamete plasma membranes, also known as prospore membranes (Figure 5C–D; Videos 6–9).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5C–D and Videos 6–9.

claim: The nuclear envelope-bound compartment outside of gamete nuclei contains nucleolar material and NPCs in budding yeast meiosis.
source: Importantly, individual sections showed that the compartment contained nucleolar material and NPCs (Figure 5E and F; Figure 5—figure supplement 2; Videos 6 and 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5E, Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 2, and Videos 6 and 8.

claim: During meiosis II, the nuclear envelope undergoes a five-way division to form four nuclei and a separate compartment containing discarded nuclear proteins in budding yeast.
source: We conclude that, during meiosis II, the nuclear envelope undergoes a five-way division to form the four nuclei and a separate compartment containing discarded nuclear proteins.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on electron microscopy observations.

claim: Throughout anaphase II, a sequestered mass of nucleoporins is constrained to a region immediately outside of nascent plasma membranes and never appears inside in budding yeast.
source: We found that, throughout anaphase II, a sequestered mass of nucleoporins was constrained to a region immediately outside of the nascent plasma membranes and never appeared inside (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The lip of developing plasma membranes marked by Don1-GFP delineates the boundary of the NPC mass during budding yeast meiosis.
source: The lip of the developing plasma membranes marked by Don1-GFP neatly delineated the boundary of the NPC mass (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: NPCs remain outside of nascent plasma membranes throughout their development during budding yeast meiosis, supporting 'exclusion' as the mechanism.
source: Live-cell microscopy confirmed that the NPCs remained outside of nascent plasma membranes throughout their development, supporting 'exclusion' as the means by which nuclear material remained outside of the developing gametes (Figure 6—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell microscopy data shown in Figure 6—figure supplements 1–2.

claim: Age-induced damage almost never enters into newly forming gametes during budding yeast meiosis.
source: This analysis revealed that age-induced damage almost never entered into newly forming gametes (Figure 6C; Figure 6—figure supplement 3; Video 10).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 3, and Video 10.

claim: Only one out of several hundred gametes inherited Hsp104-associated protein aggregates during budding yeast meiosis.
source: Only one out of several hundred gametes inherited the Hsp104-associated protein aggregates (Figure 6D; Video 11); strikingly, this Hsp104 punctum persisted after gamete maturation, suggesting that the elimination of age-associated damage is dependent on its prior exclusion.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D and Video 11.

claim: The elimination of age-associated damage is dependent on its prior exclusion from gametes during budding yeast meiosis.
source: Only one out of several hundred gametes inherited the Hsp104-associated protein aggregates (Figure 6D; Video 11); strikingly, this Hsp104 punctum persisted after gamete maturation, suggesting that the elimination of age-associated damage is dependent on its prior exclusion.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that an inherited protein aggregate persisted after gamete maturation.

claim: The disappearance of NPCs and age-associated protein aggregates coincides with the onset of vacuolar lysis during budding yeast gametogenesis.
source: We found that both events coincided with the onset of vacuolar lysis (Figure 7A–D; Figure 7—source data 1–2; Videos 12–13).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A–D and Videos 12–13.

claim: Free GFP accumulates in wild-type budding yeast cells 12 hours after meiosis induction, consistent with vacuolar proteases driving the elimination of Nup84 and Nup170.
source: We found that free GFP accumulated in wild-type cells 12 hours after meiosis induction, consistent with vacuolar proteases driving the elimination of Nup84 and Nup170 (Figure 7E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 7E–F.

claim: The degradation of Nup84 and Nup170 depends on the meiotic transcription factor Ndt80 in budding yeast.
source: Importantly, we confirmed that the degradation of both nucleoporins depends on the meiotic transcription factor Ndt80.
evidence: The claim is based on the comparison of wild-type and ndt80Δ cells shown in Figure 7E–F.

claim: Ndt80 is a master transcription factor necessary for meiotic divisions and gamete maturation in budding yeast.
source: Ndt80 is a master transcription factor necessary for the meiotic divisions and gamete maturation (Xu et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Xu et al., 1995).

claim: In the absence of NDT80, budding yeast cells exhibit a prolonged arrest during prophase I and fail to undergo vacuolar lysis.
source: In the absence of NDT80, cells exhibit a prolonged arrest during prophase I and fail to undergo vacuolar lysis (Eastwood et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Eastwood et al., 2012).

claim: Mega-autophagy is the probable degradation mechanism for NPCs and nuclear senescence factors during budding yeast gametogenesis.
source: Altogether, these analyses highlight mega-autophagy as the probable degradation mechanism for NPCs and nuclear senescence factors.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the coincidence of NPC/aggregate disappearance with vacuolar lysis and the dependence on Ndt80.

claim: In spo21Δ budding yeast cells, nucleoporins remain around chromosomes during anaphase II instead of being sequestered away.
source: We found that, in spo21Δ cells, nucleoporins remained around chromosomes during anaphase II instead of being sequestered away (Figure 8A–B; Figure 8—source data 1; Video 14).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A–B and Video 14.

claim: SPO21 is required for the conversion of the spindle pole body from a microtubule-nucleation center to a membrane-nucleation center during budding yeast meiosis II.
source: Plasma membrane development is initiated from the cytoplasmic face of the spindle pole body, which is converted from a microtubule-nucleation center to a membrane-nucleation center during meiosis II (Knop and Strasser, 2000). SPO21 (also known as MPC70) is required for this conversion event, and its deletion completely inhibits de novo plasma membrane formation (Knop and Strasser, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Knop and Strasser, 2000).

claim: Deletion of SPO21 completely inhibits de novo plasma membrane formation during budding yeast meiosis.
source: SPO21 (also known as MPC70) is required for this conversion event, and its deletion completely inhibits de novo plasma membrane formation (Knop and Strasser, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Knop and Strasser, 2000).

claim: In budding yeast cells with fewer than four gamete plasma membranes, only nuclei devoid of plasma membranes are enriched for NPCs.
source: Under such conditions, we found that the gamete nuclei displayed reciprocal localization of plasma membranes and NPCs: only the nuclei that were devoid of plasma membranes were enriched for NPCs (Figure 8C–E; Figure 8—source data 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C–E.

claim: Deletion of the leading edge complex organizing member Ssp1 results in the formation of misshapen plasma membranes during budding yeast meiosis.
source: Specifically, the absence of the organizing member Ssp1 or simultaneous deletion of the Ady3 and Irc10 subunits results in the formation of misshapen plasma membranes (Lam et al., 2014; Moreno-Borchart et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Lam et al., 2014; Moreno-Borchart et al., 2001).

claim: Simultaneous deletion of Ady3 and Irc10 results in the formation of misshapen plasma membranes during budding yeast meiosis.
source: Specifically, the absence of the organizing member Ssp1 or simultaneous deletion of the Ady3 and Irc10 subunits results in the formation of misshapen plasma membranes (Lam et al., 2014; Moreno-Borchart et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Lam et al., 2014; Moreno-Borchart et al., 2001).

claim: Both ssp1Δ and ady3Δ irc10Δ budding yeast cells have defective NPC sequestration, with NPCs often remaining partially around anaphase II nuclei.
source: We found that both ssp1Δ and ady3Δ irc10Δ cells had defective NPC sequestration, with NPCs often remaining partially around anaphase II nuclei (Figure 8F; Figure 8—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8F and Figure 8—figure supplements 1–2.

claim: The boundary of NPC removal from nuclei corresponds to the extent of plasma membrane formation in ssp1Δ and ady3Δ irc10Δ budding yeast cells.
source: The boundary of NPC removal from the nuclei was marked by constrictions in the DAPI or histone signal and corresponded to the extent of plasma membrane formation (Figure 8F; Figure 8—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8F and Figure 8—figure supplements 1–2.

claim: NPC sequestration and exclusion are driven by the development of plasma membranes around nascent gamete nuclei in budding yeast.
source: Taken together, these data support the conclusion that NPC sequestration and exclusion are driven by the development of plasma membranes around nascent gamete nuclei.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the genetic and imaging experiments with plasma membrane mutants.

claim: In spo21Δ budding yeast cells, there is a dramatic increase in the association of protein aggregates with chromosomes during anaphase II compared to wild-type cells (48% vs. 0%).
source: In comparison to wild-type cells, we found that spo21Δ mutants exhibited a dramatic increase in the association of protein aggregates with chromosomes during anaphase II (48% vs. 0%; Figure 9A–B; Figure 9—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 9A–B.

claim: In spo21Δ budding yeast cells, protein aggregates always co-localize with the nuclear envelope, regardless of whether they are sequestered away from chromosomes.
source: Regardless of whether or not the protein aggregate was sequestered away from chromosomes in spo21∆ cells, the protein aggregates always co-localized with the nuclear envelope, as marked by NPCs (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: Without nascent plasma membranes, protein aggregates appear randomly distributed along the nuclear periphery in budding yeast.
source: Thus, without the nascent plasma membranes, protein aggregates appeared randomly distributed along the nuclear periphery.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that protein aggregates co-localize with the nuclear envelope in spo21Δ cells.

claim: In 39% of young spo21Δ budding yeast cells, nucleoli fail to be sequestered in meiosis II and instead co-segregate with chromosomes.
source: We found that in 39% of spo21Δ cells, nucleoli failed to be sequestered in meiosis II and instead co-segregated with chromosomes (Figure 9C–D; Figure 9—source data 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 9C–D.

claim: None of the wild-type budding yeast cells display nucleolar co-segregation with chromosomes during meiosis II.
source: In contrast, none of the wild-type cells displayed this behavior.
evidence: The claim is based on the comparison with spo21Δ cells described in the text.

claim: Nsr1 remains co-localized to the nuclear envelope in spo21Δ budding yeast cells in a similar manner to protein aggregates.
source: Furthermore, Nsr1 remained co-localized to the nuclear envelope in spo21Δ cells in a similar manner to protein aggregates (Figure 9—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 2.

claim: Meiotic exclusion of age-induced protein aggregates and nucleolar material is coupled to a nuclear remodeling event driven by gamete plasma membrane formation in budding yeast.
source: Altogether, these findings support the notion that meiotic exclusion of age-induced protein aggregates and nucleolar material is coupled to a nuclear remodeling event that is driven by gamete plasma membrane formation.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the experiments with spo21Δ cells.

claim: De novo plasma membrane growth is required for the sequestration of nuclear material during budding yeast meiosis.
source: We further show that de novo plasma membrane growth is required for the sequestration of nuclear material (Figure 10).
evidence: The claim is a summary of the findings shown in Figure 10 and throughout the study.

claim: A meiosis-specific nuclear remodeling event physically separates age-induced cellular damage away from gametes in budding yeast.
source: Together, our findings define a meiosis-specific nuclear remodeling event that physically separates age-induced cellular damage away from gametes and highlights its role in cellular rejuvenation.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: Strong association with chromatin may be one way to mediate the selective inheritance of nuclear proteins into gametes during budding yeast meiosis.
source: Strong association with chromatin, as in the case for histones, Cfi1 and Prp20, may be one way to mediate the selective inheritance of nuclear proteins into gametes (Aebi et al., 1990; Dilworth et al., 2005; Li et al., 2003; Straight et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the observed retention of certain nuclear proteins and supported by citations (Aebi et al., 1990; Dilworth et al., 2005; Li et al., 2003; Straight et al., 1999).

claim: Strong association with NPCs may facilitate sequestration of nuclear material during budding yeast meiosis.
source: On the other hand, strong association with NPCs may facilitate sequestration – for example, extrachromosomal rDNA circles have been shown to interact with NPCs in mitotic cells (Denoth-Lippuner et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the known interaction of rDNA circles with NPCs, supported by a citation (Denoth-Lippuner et al., 2014).

claim: The fraction of discarded nucleolar proteins is higher in aged budding yeast cells than young cells.
source: However, the observation that the fraction of discarded nucleolar proteins is higher in aged cells than young cells is consistent with the possibility that damaged nucleolar proteins are selectively enriched in the sequestered material.
evidence: The claim is based on the quantification shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Damaged nucleolar proteins may be selectively enriched in the sequestered material during budding yeast meiosis.
source: However, the observation that the fraction of discarded nucleolar proteins is higher in aged cells than young cells is consistent with the possibility that damaged nucleolar proteins are selectively enriched in the sequestered material.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the observation that more nucleolar protein is sequestered in aged cells.

claim: Nuclear basket nucleoporins are more dynamic than core nucleoporins in budding yeast.
source: Consistent with this finding, nuclear basket nucleoporins have been shown to be more dynamic than core nucleoporins (Denning et al., 2001; Dilworth et al., 2001; Niepel et al., 2013) and sub-populations of NPCs without certain nuclear basket nucleoporins are present near the nucleolus (Galy et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Denning et al., 2001; Dilworth et al., 2001; Niepel et al., 2013).

claim: Sub-populations of NPCs without certain nuclear basket nucleoporins are present near the nucleolus in budding yeast.
source: Consistent with this finding, nuclear basket nucleoporins have been shown to be more dynamic than core nucleoporins (Denning et al., 2001; Dilworth et al., 2001; Niepel et al., 2013) and sub-populations of NPCs without certain nuclear basket nucleoporins are present near the nucleolus (Galy et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Galy et al., 2004).

claim: The nuclear basket segregates with gamete nuclei through re-association with chromatin during budding yeast meiosis.
source: We propose that the nuclear basket segregates with gamete nuclei through re-association with chromatin, which in turn facilitates the formation of new NPCs.
evidence: The claim is a proposal based on the observed behavior of nuclear basket nucleoporins.

claim: In Aspergillus nidulans and vertebrates, the nuclear basket nucleoporin Nup2 and its metazoan ortholog Nup50 associate with dividing chromatin during mitosis and contribute to the segregation of NPCs into daughter nuclei.
source: In both the fungus Asperilligus nidulans and vertebrates, the nuclear basket nucleoporin Nup2 and its metazoan ortholog Nup50 associate with dividing chromatin during mitosis and contribute to the segregation of NPCs into daughter nuclei (Dultz et al., 2008; Markossian et al., 2015; Suresh et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Dultz et al., 2008; Markossian et al., 2015; Suresh et al., 2017).

claim: The nuclear basket nucleoporins Nup1 and Nup60 have innate membrane binding and shaping capabilities.
source: The nuclear basket nucleoporins Nup1 and Nup60 have innate membrane binding and shaping capabilities, making them attractive candidates to initiate insertion of new NPCs (Mészáros et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Mészáros et al., 2015).

claim: Deletion of non-essential nuclear basket nucleoporins results in reduced sporulation efficiency and impaired gamete viability in budding yeast.
source: Indeed, deletion of non-essential nuclear basket nucleoporins results in reduced sporulation efficiency and impaired gamete viability, supporting an important functional role during the meiotic program (Chu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Chu et al., 2017).

claim: Deletion of meiosis-specific septins (spr3Δ and spr28Δ) does not grossly alter NPC or protein aggregate sequestration in budding yeast, beyond impacting plasma membrane morphology.
source: In meiosis, deletion of meiosis-specific septins (spr3Δ and spr28Δ; De Virgilio et al., 1996; Fares et al., 1996; Ozsarac et al., 1995) and leading edge complex components (ady3Δ, irc10Δ, and don1Δ; Knop and Strasser, 2000; Lam et al., 2014; Moreno-Borchart et al., 2001) does not grossly alter NPC or protein aggregate sequestration, beyond impacting plasma membrane morphology (Figure 8F; Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8F and Supplementary file 5, and by citations to published research (De Virgilio et al., 1996; Fares et al., 1996; Ozsarac et al., 1995).

claim: Deletion of leading edge complex components (ady3Δ, irc10Δ, and don1Δ) does not grossly alter NPC or protein aggregate sequestration in budding yeast, beyond impacting plasma membrane morphology.
source: In meiosis, deletion of meiosis-specific septins (spr3Δ and spr28Δ; De Virgilio et al., 1996; Fares et al., 1996; Ozsarac et al., 1995) and leading edge complex components (ady3Δ, irc10Δ, and don1Δ; Knop and Strasser, 2000; Lam et al., 2014; Moreno-Borchart et al., 2001) does not grossly alter NPC or protein aggregate sequestration, beyond impacting plasma membrane morphology (Figure 8F; Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8F and Supplementary file 5, and by citations to published research (Knop and Strasser, 2000; Lam et al., 2014; Moreno-Borchart et al., 2001).

claim: Some core nucleoporins may be able to overcome the physical or diffusion barrier imposed by the plasma membrane during budding yeast meiosis.
source: This raises the intriguing possibility that some core nucleoporins may be able to overcome the physical or diffusion barrier imposed by the plasma membrane.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the observation that some nucleoporins re-appear around gamete nuclei.

claim: In mitosis, an active transmission mechanism involving the nucleoporin Nsp1 is required for NPCs to pass the bud neck diffusion barrier and enter into daughter cells in budding yeast.
source: In mitosis, an active transmission mechanism involving the nucleoporin Nsp1 is required for NPCs to pass the bud neck diffusion barrier and enter into daughter cells (Colombi et al., 2013; Makio et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Colombi et al., 2013; Makio et al., 2013).

claim: Daughter-inherited NPCs are modified by the deacetylase Hos3 as they pass through the bud neck in budding yeast mitosis, resulting in the formation of a daughter nucleus with distinct cell-cycle behaviors from the mother nucleus.
source: Further, daughter-inherited NPCs are modified by the deacetylase Hos3 as they pass through the bud neck, resulting in the formation of a daughter nucleus with distinct cell-cycle behaviors from the mother nucleus (Kumar et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Kumar et al., 2018).

claim: Transmission through the leading edge of the gamete plasma membrane might provide an opportunity for any inherited NPCs to acquire gamete-specific modifications and functions during budding yeast meiosis.
source: Transmission through the leading edge of the gamete plasma membrane might similarly provide an opportunity for any inherited NPCs to acquire gamete-specific modifications and functions.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the analogy with mitotic NPC modification.

claim: The endonuclease G homolog, Nuc1, is released from mitochondria during mega-autophagy in budding yeast.
source: The endonuclease G homolog, Nuc1, is released from mitochondria during mega-autophagy and therefore could be responsible for the elimination of rDNA circles (Eastwood et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Eastwood et al., 2012).

claim: Nuc1 could be responsible for the elimination of rDNA circles during budding yeast gametogenesis.
source: The endonuclease G homolog, Nuc1, is released from mitochondria during mega-autophagy and therefore could be responsible for the elimination of rDNA circles (Eastwood et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the known release of Nuc1 during mega-autophagy.

claim: The sequestration of NPCs in budding yeast meiosis is similar to a NPC reorganization event observed in the spermatogenesis of metazoans, including humans.
source: Importantly, the sequestration of NPCs in budding yeast meiosis is similar to a NPC reorganization event observed in the spermatogenesis of metazoans, including humans (Fawcett and Chemes, 1979; Ho, 2010; Troyer and Schwager, 1982).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Fawcett and Chemes, 1979; Ho, 2010; Troyer and Schwager, 1982).

claim: In metazoan spermatogenesis, acrosome formation corresponds to the redistribution of nuclear pores to the caudal end of the nucleus, coincident with chromatin condensation and elimination of un-inherited nuclear material.
source: In this context, acrosome formation, potentially akin to gamete plasma membrane formation, corresponds to the redistribution of nuclear pores to the caudal end of the nucleus, coincident with chromatin condensation and elimination of un-inherited nuclear material.
evidence: The claim is based on the comparison with metazoan spermatogenesis described in the text.

claim: In C. elegans gametogenesis, oocyte maturation involves the elimination of age-induced protein aggregates by lysosomal activation.
source: In C. elegans gametogenesis, oocyte maturation involves the elimination of age-induced protein aggregates by lysosomal activation (Bohnert and Kenyon, 2017; Goudeau and Aguilaniu, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Bohnert and Kenyon, 2017; Goudeau and Aguilaniu, 2010).

claim: In aged budding yeast cells carrying TetR-GFP without the tetO-rDNA array, the GFP signal remains diffuse throughout meiosis.
source: In aged cells carrying TetR-GFP without the tetO-rDNA array, the GFP signal remained diffuse throughout meiosis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), confirming that the extrachromosomal GFP puncta were due to sequestered rDNA circles as opposed to TetR-GFP aggregation.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The rRNA processing factors Nop1 and Nhp2 are partially sequestered away from chromosomes during gametogenesis in budding yeast.
source: A previous study found that two other rRNA processing factors, the fibrillarin homolog Nop1 and the high mobility group protein Nhp2, are partially sequestered away from chromosomes during gametogenesis (Fuchs and Loidl, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Fuchs and Loidl, 2004).
